title: Trees & Heaps
tagline: Hierarchical structure that makes searching O(log n) — and heaps that always know the min or max in O(1).

sections.content:
Open the file explorer on your computer. Each folder can contain other folders, which can contain more folders — a structure that branches outward rather than marching forward in a line. That branching shape is a **tree**, and it is one of the most important data structures in all of computing. The Document Object Model (DOM) that your browser uses to render web pages is a tree. The Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) your JavaScript engine builds before executing code is a tree. The B-tree indexes inside PostgreSQL and MySQL that make database lookups fast are trees. Filesystems, compilers, JSON, XML, decision algorithms in machine learning — trees are everywhere.

What makes trees so powerful? Unlike arrays and linked lists, which are **linear** — one element after the next — trees **branch**. Each node can have multiple children, which can each have multiple children, and so on. This branching creates a logarithmic relationship between depth and coverage: a balanced binary tree of depth 20 can hold over a million nodes. That means finding any node requires at most 20 comparisons — even with a million entries. That is the O(log n) advantage that makes binary search trees an essential tool.

A **heap** is a specialised tree with a very different personality. Where a binary search tree maintains a strict left-smaller-right-larger ordering everywhere, a heap is content with a much weaker rule: the parent is always larger (max-heap) or smaller (min-heap) than its children. It does not care whether the left child is bigger or smaller than the right child. That relaxed attitude is the source of its power: a heap can be stored as a flat array with no pointers at all, and it can always give you the maximum or minimum element in O(1). When you need to repeatedly pull out the most urgent item in a task queue, find the nearest neighbour in a graph algorithm, or merge sorted streams, the heap is your tool.

This chapter covers both structures from first principles: how trees are defined, how to traverse them, why BSTs degenerate and how self-balancing trees fix that, then the full mechanics of heap insert and extract with the array arithmetic that makes it work.

sections.title: A Family Tree and a Tournament Bracket
sections.content:
A **binary tree** is like a family tree where each person has at most two children. The topmost ancestor is the root. People at the bottom with no children are leaves. Internal nodes are everyone in between. The **depth** of a person is how many generations removed they are from the ancestor at the top; the **height** of the tree is the depth of the deepest leaf.

A **binary search tree (BST)** adds one precise rule on top of the family-tree structure: every person on the left branch has a value smaller than their ancestor, and every person on the right branch has a larger value. To find someone, you start at the root and ask at each step: is the person I am looking for smaller or larger than the current person? Smaller — go left; larger — go right. Each question eliminates an entire half of the remaining people. After 20 steps you have narrowed a million-person tree to a single candidate.

A **heap** is better understood as a tournament bracket. In a max-heap, imagine a tournament where the winner of each match is the player with the higher score, and they advance upward. After all matches, the champion at the top is guaranteed to be the overall highest scorer. When the champion retires, the bracket reorganises in a clever way: it does not replay the entire tournament (that would be O(n log n)). Instead, it promotes a replacement, runs a small number of matches along a single path from top to bottom — at most log₂(n) matches — and the new champion emerges in O(log n). You always know who is in first place, and each extraction is cheap.

sections.title: Binary Trees: Structure and Terminology
sections.content:
Before studying algorithms, the vocabulary needs to be precise.

A **binary tree** is a tree where every node has at most two children, called the **left child** and **right child**. A node with no children is a **leaf**. A node with at least one child is an **internal node**. The single node at the top with no parent is the **root**.

The **height** of a tree is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. A tree with a single node has height 0. An empty tree has height -1 by convention (though some textbooks say 0 — be aware of this inconsistency in references).

A tree is **full** if every node has 0 or 2 children (no node has exactly 1). A tree is **complete** if every level is fully filled except possibly the last, which is filled from the left side. A tree is **perfect** if all internal nodes have exactly 2 children and all leaves are at the same depth. A perfect binary tree of height h has exactly 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes.

The distinction between complete and perfect matters enormously for heaps: the **complete** property ensures the tree can be packed without gaps into a flat array, which is the key trick that lets heaps avoid pointer overhead.

sections.caption: Binary Search Tree with values [8,3,10,1,6,14,4,7]. At every node, all left-subtree values are smaller and all right-subtree values are larger. In-order traversal yields [1,3,4,6,7,8,10,14] — sorted ascending.

sections.title: The BST Property and Why It Enables Binary Search
sections.content:
A **binary search tree** enforces a single invariant: for any node N, every value in N's left subtree is strictly less than N's value, and every value in N's right subtree is strictly greater. This must hold not just for immediate children but for the entire subtree — a common mistake is to check only the direct parent-child relationship and miss deeper violations.

Search exploits this invariant beautifully. To find a value `x` starting at the root:
- If `x === node.value`, return found.
- If `x < node.value`, recurse into the left subtree (right subtree cannot contain `x`).
- If `x > node.value`, recurse into the right subtree.

Each step eliminates one entire side of the tree. In a **balanced** tree — one where the height is O(log n) — this means at most log₂(n) comparisons. With n = 1,000,000 nodes, that is at most 20 steps.

Insertion works similarly: follow the search path until you fall off the tree, then attach the new node at that position. Deletion is the trickiest operation: removing a leaf is trivial; removing a node with one child just splices that child up; removing a node with two children requires finding the **in-order successor** (the smallest value in the right subtree) or **in-order predecessor** (largest in the left), swapping values, and deleting the successor/predecessor instead — which has at most one child.

All three operations run in O(h) where h is the height of the tree. The critical insight is what h is: in a balanced tree h = O(log n), but nothing in the basic BST definition guarantees balance.

sections.title: The Degenerate Tree Problem and Self-Balancing Trees
sections.content:
Here is the BST's Achilles heel: if you insert elements in sorted order — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, … — each new element always goes to the right. The tree becomes a single long chain with height n, and search degrades to O(n), exactly the same as scanning a linked list. This is not a rare edge case; it is what happens whenever data arrives pre-sorted, which happens constantly in real systems (timestamps, auto-increment IDs, alphabetically sorted imports).

The fix is **self-balancing** trees, which automatically restructure after insertions and deletions to maintain O(log n) height. The two most important families:

**AVL trees** (Adelson-Velsky and Landis, 1962) maintain the **AVL property**: for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. After any insert or delete, the tree checks this property and, if violated, performs one or two **rotations** — a local restructuring that adjusts parent-child relationships without breaking the BST property. AVL trees guarantee height ≤ 1.44 log₂(n), making all operations strictly O(log n). They tend to be more strictly balanced than Red-Black trees but require slightly more rotations on insert.

**Red-Black trees** (Rudolf Bayer, 1972; the name comes from 1978) colour each node red or black and maintain five invariants that together guarantee height ≤ 2 log₂(n + 1). They are less strictly balanced than AVL trees but require fewer rotations on average. Java's `TreeMap`, C++ `std::map`, Linux kernel interval trees, and many language runtime implementations use Red-Black trees. Python's `sortedcontainers` library implements a similar idea with a sorted list of sorted lists (a B-tree variant).

For most interview purposes, you do not need to implement a self-balancing tree — but you absolutely need to know they exist, why they are needed, and that they give guaranteed O(log n) for all operations.

sections.title: Tree Traversals: Four Ways to Visit Every Node
sections.content:
A **traversal** visits every node exactly once in a defined order. For a binary tree, four traversals are standard, each with distinct use cases.

**In-order** (left → node → right): For a BST, this visits nodes in ascending sorted order — the direct consequence of the BST property. Useful for printing sorted data, implementing a sorted iterator, or verifying BST correctness.

**Pre-order** (node → left → right): Visits the root before its subtrees. Useful for **serialising** a tree to a string (you can reconstruct the exact same BST from a pre-order sequence) and for **cloning** a tree (create the node before creating its children).

**Post-order** (left → right → node): Visits children before the parent. Useful for **deleting** a tree (free children before the parent), computing **directory sizes** (sum subfolder sizes before reporting the parent folder), and evaluating **expression trees** (compute operands before applying the operator).

**Level-order** (breadth-first, BFS): Visits all nodes at depth 0, then all at depth 1, then depth 2, and so on, using a queue. Useful for finding the shortest path in an unweighted tree, printing a tree level by level, and finding the minimum depth.

All four traversals are O(n) — every node is visited exactly once. The recursive implementations of the first three are elegant and short. The iterative versions require an explicit stack (DFS) or queue (BFS). In interviews, knowing how to implement iterative in-order traversal with an explicit stack is a common test of understanding.

sections.title: Binary Heaps: The Complete Tree Stored as an Array
sections.content:
A **binary heap** looks like a binary tree on paper but is actually stored as a flat array — no `left` or `right` pointer fields at all. This is possible because a heap is always a **complete** binary tree: every level is fully populated except possibly the last, and the last level is filled from left to right with no gaps. That no-gap rule means every node's position in a breadth-first enumeration is a well-defined integer index.

For a 0-indexed array, the arithmetic is simple and beautiful:
- Node at index `i` has its **left child** at index `2i + 1`
- Node at index `i` has its **right child** at index `2i + 2`
- Node at index `i` has its **parent** at index `Math.floor((i - 1) / 2)`

No pointers, no node objects, no memory allocation per insert. Just an array and three arithmetic formulas. This is why heaps are cache-friendly and fast in practice — array traversal is linear in memory, CPU prefetchers love it.

The **heap property** is separate from the structural completeness: in a **max-heap**, every parent is greater than or equal to both its children. In a **min-heap**, every parent is less than or equal to both children. Note what the heap property does NOT say: it says nothing about the relationship between siblings. The left child might be larger or smaller than the right child — the heap does not care. This is a weaker invariant than a BST's, but it is all you need to efficiently find the maximum or minimum.

sections.title: Heap Insert: Heapify-Up (Bubble Up)
sections.content:
To insert a new value into a heap:
1. **Append** the new value at the end of the array. This preserves the complete-tree structural property — you are adding to the leftmost available position on the bottom level.
2. **Heapify-up** (also called bubble-up or sift-up): compare the new value with its parent. If the new value violates the heap property (e.g., in a max-heap, new value > parent), swap them. Repeat with the new parent, continuing upward until the heap property is satisfied or you reach the root.

Each iteration moves up one level, and the tree has at most log₂(n) levels, so heapify-up is **O(log n)** in the worst case. On average it is even faster because most insertions settle near the bottom after just a few swaps.

An important correctness note: when you swap a node upward, you only need to check the node against its new parent — you never need to check siblings. This is because the siblings were already satisfying the heap property before the insert; the only new violation possible is along the path from the inserted node to the root.

sections.title: Heap Extract: Heapify-Down (Sift Down)
sections.content:
Extracting the minimum (from a min-heap) or maximum (from a max-heap) means removing the root — but you cannot just delete the root and leave a hole at the top of the array. The procedure:
1. **Save** the root value (this is what we are returning).
2. **Move** the last element in the array to index 0 (the root position), then remove the last element. The array shrinks by one, structural completeness is preserved.
3. **Heapify-down** (also called sift-down or bubble-down): the new root is likely violating the heap property. Compare it with its two children. Find the child that would restore order if swapped (the larger child in a max-heap, the smaller in a min-heap). If that child already satisfies the heap property (parent is already ≤ both children in a min-heap), stop. Otherwise swap and repeat at the new position.

Heapify-down also runs in **O(log n)** — at most one swap per level, and there are log₂(n) levels.

Peeking at the minimum or maximum — without removing it — is **O(1)**: just read index 0 of the array.

**Building a heap from an existing array** (heapify) can be done in O(n), which is better than inserting n elements one by one (O(n log n)). The trick: start from the last non-leaf node (at index `Math.floor(n/2) - 1`) and call heapify-down on each node going backward to the root. Nodes near the bottom of the tree (the majority) sift down a small distance; nodes near the top sift down farther but there are exponentially fewer of them. The total work is a geometric series that sums to O(n). This O(n) heapification is also the foundation of **heap sort**, which sorts an array in O(n log n) with O(1) extra space.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `push` loop runs at most log₂(n) times because the tree has log₂(n) levels — one swap per level at most. The `pop` sift-down loop also runs at most log₂(n) times. The `buildMinHeap` function is O(n): despite calling siftDown n/2 times, most nodes are near the bottom and sift a small distance. The total work is bounded by the sum n/4×1 + n/8×2 + n/16×3 + … which converges to O(n).

sections.title: Priority Queues and Real-World Applications
sections.content:
A **priority queue** is an abstract data type that supports two operations: insert an element with a priority, and extract the element with the highest (or lowest) priority. Binary heaps are the standard implementation because they deliver O(log n) insert and extract with O(1) peek and O(n) build.

**Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm** uses a min-heap as its core. The algorithm maintains a heap of (distance, node) pairs. It always extracts the node with the smallest current known distance, relaxes its edges, and re-inserts updated distances. With a binary heap, each extraction is O(log V) and each edge relaxation is O(log V), giving overall O((V + E) log V). Without a heap — scanning a simple array for the minimum — the algorithm runs in O(V²), which is painfully slow on large graphs.

**A* search** (used in game pathfinding, GPS routing, and robotics) also uses a min-heap ordered by f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g is the cost to reach the node and h is the heuristic estimate to the goal.

**Operating system schedulers** use priority queues to decide which process to run next. In a real-time system, the highest-priority ready task runs first; the heap ensures O(log n) scheduling decisions.

**The k-smallest / k-largest problem** is a classic interview pattern. To find the k largest elements in a stream of n numbers, maintain a min-heap of size k. For each incoming number, if it is larger than the heap's minimum (root), pop the root and push the new number. After processing all n numbers, the heap contains the k largest. Time: O(n log k), which is much better than sorting all n when k is small.

**Merge k sorted lists** (a common interview problem) is elegantly solved with a min-heap: insert the first element of each list into a heap, then repeatedly extract the minimum and insert the next element from the same list. O(n log k) where n is total elements and k is number of lists.

sections.title: Heap Sort: An In-Place O(n log n) Sort with O(1) Extra Space
sections.content:
Heap sort is a comparison sort that uses the heap data structure to achieve O(n log n) time with O(1) extra space — unlike merge sort, which needs O(n) auxiliary space, and unlike quicksort, which has an O(n²) worst case.

**Phase 1: Build max-heap** from the input array in O(n) using the heapify trick (sift-down from the last non-leaf to the root).

**Phase 2: Sort by repeated extraction**: The root (index 0) is the maximum. Swap it with the last element, shrink the heap boundary by one (the last element is now in its final sorted position), and sift-down the new root to restore the heap property. Repeat n-1 times.

Result: the array is sorted in ascending order in O(n log n) total. Phase 1 is O(n) and Phase 2 is O(n log n) — the Phase 2 term dominates.

Despite its guarantees, heap sort is rarely used in practice for general sorting. It has poor **cache performance** (heapify-down accesses memory in a non-sequential pattern; parent at index i, children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 — these jump around), while quicksort with good pivot selection has better locality and smaller constant factors. Introsort (used in many standard libraries) starts with quicksort and switches to heap sort when recursion depth exceeds a threshold — combining the best of both.

sections.title: Common Mistakes, Edge Cases, and Interview Traps
sections.content:
**BST degeneration**: The single most common BST mistake in interviews is claiming O(log n) without acknowledging the balanced-tree assumption. Always say 'O(log n) for a balanced BST; O(n) worst case without balancing.' Then mention AVL or Red-Black trees as the fix.

**Off-by-one in heap index arithmetic**: The formulas change depending on whether you use 0-indexed or 1-indexed arrays. In a 1-indexed heap: left child = 2i, right child = 2i+1, parent = floor(i/2). In a 0-indexed heap: left = 2i+1, right = 2i+2, parent = floor((i-1)/2). Mixing up the two is a very common interview mistake — be consistent and double-check.

**Heap is not sorted**: A heap gives you efficient access to the minimum or maximum, but the rest of the elements are not in any particular order. Do not assume `heap[1]` is the second smallest — it might not be. Only the root's O(1) access guarantee is valid.

**BST equality**: The BST property is typically defined as left < parent and right > parent (strict), meaning no duplicates. Some implementations allow duplicates by going right on equal values. Be clear about which convention you are using.

**Deleting from the middle of a heap**: This is O(log n) but requires finding the element first (O(n) without an auxiliary index map). Standard heap implementations (JavaScript priority queues, Python's `heapq`) do not support arbitrary deletion efficiently. If you need this, you typically use a **lazy deletion** strategy: mark the element as deleted and skip it when it reaches the top.

**Tree height vs depth**: height is measured from a node downward to its deepest leaf; depth is measured from the root downward to the node. The height of the tree = height of the root = depth of the deepest leaf. These are often confused in problems asking for 'the height of the tree' vs 'the depth of a node'.

**Recursion stack depth**: For a BST with n nodes in worst case, recursive traversal uses O(n) stack space. For large trees (n = 10⁶), this can cause stack overflow. Iterative versions with an explicit stack avoid this.

**Historical context:** The binary heap was invented by J. W. J. Williams in 1964 specifically for the heap sort algorithm, published in the Communications of the ACM. The name 'heap' for both the data structure and the region of memory where dynamic allocation occurs is an unfortunate collision — they are completely unrelated. Binary search trees were studied as early as the 1950s; the first self-balancing variant (AVL tree) was published by Soviet mathematicians Georgy Adelson-Velsky and Evgenii Landis in 1962. Red-Black trees emerged from Rudolf Bayer's 1972 symmetric binary B-tree and were given the red-black colouring by Leonidas Guibas and Robert Sedgewick in 1978.

**Interview pattern recognition:** When a problem says 'find the k largest / k smallest elements,' reach for a heap of size k — O(n log k). When it says 'process events in order of priority,' reach for a heap. When it says 'find the median of a stream,' think two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half, a min-heap for the upper half — the median is always at one of the two roots. When a problem involves a tree and asks for a sorted result, think in-order traversal of a BST. When it asks for the shortest path in a weighted graph, Dijkstra plus a min-heap. The heap shows up surprisingly often once you learn to see it.

items: A **binary search tree** maintains the invariant that all left-subtree values are less than a node and all right-subtree values are greater, enabling O(log n) search, insert, and delete in a balanced tree — but O(n) in a degenerate (sorted-insertion) tree. Self-balancing variants (AVL, Red-Black) guarantee O(log n) always.

The four traversal orders each serve a different purpose: **in-order** produces sorted output from a BST; **pre-order** serialises or clones a tree; **post-order** evaluates expression trees and computes bottom-up aggregations; **level-order** (BFS) finds shortest paths and processes nodes layer by layer.

A **binary heap** is a complete binary tree stored as a flat array using index arithmetic — left child at 2i+1, right child at 2i+2, parent at floor((i-1)/2). No pointer fields are needed. This makes heaps cache-friendly and memory-efficient.

Heap **insert** (append + heapify-up) and **extract** (save root, move last to root, heapify-down) are both O(log n). Peeking at the min or max is O(1). Building a heap from an unsorted array is O(n) via the sift-down-from-last-non-leaf trick.

The heap is the canonical backing structure for **priority queues**, powering Dijkstra's algorithm, A* search, OS schedulers, and the k-largest/k-smallest streaming pattern — O(n log k) is much better than O(n log n) sorting when k is small.

**Heap sort** achieves O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space by combining O(n) heapify with n iterations of extract-max, but poor cache locality makes it slower in practice than quicksort despite the same asymptotic complexity.

Key misconception to avoid: **a heap is not a sorted array**. Only the root position (O(1) access) carries the min/max guarantee; the remaining elements satisfy only the weak parent-child heap property and can appear in any order relative to each other.

quiz.question: What is the BST property, stated precisely?
options: Every node has exactly two children
The root always holds the maximum value
For every node N, all values in N's left subtree are less than N and all values in N's right subtree are greater
All nodes at the same depth have equal values
quiz.explanation: The BST property must hold for the entire subtree, not just the immediate children. This invariant enables binary search: at each node you eliminate an entire half of the remaining tree based on one comparison.

quiz.question: Which traversal order produces sorted ascending output when applied to a BST?
options: Pre-order (node → left → right)
In-order (left → node → right)
Post-order (left → right → node)
Level-order (breadth-first)
quiz.explanation: In-order traversal visits the left subtree (all smaller values), then the current node, then the right subtree (all larger values). Because this pattern recurses through the entire BST, it produces all values in ascending sorted order.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of BST search, and when does it occur?
options: O(log n) — the BST guarantees balance by definition
O(n) — when elements are inserted in sorted order, the tree degenerates into a linear chain
O(n²) — duplicate values cause quadratic backtracking
O(1) — BST uses hashing for direct access
quiz.explanation: Inserting elements in sorted order (e.g. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 …) forces every new node to the right, producing a chain of height n. Search must then scan the entire chain — O(n). Self-balancing trees (AVL, Red-Black) prevent this by maintaining O(log n) height.

quiz.question: In a binary heap stored in a 0-indexed array, what is the index of the left child of the node at index i?
options: 2i
quiz.explanation: For a 0-indexed heap: left child = 2i + 1, right child = 2i + 2, parent = floor((i-1)/2). These formulas come from the breadth-first enumeration of a complete binary tree. Note that 1-indexed heaps use left = 2i, right = 2i+1, parent = floor(i/2) — a common source of bugs when mixing conventions.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of peeking at the minimum value in a min-heap, and why?
options: O(n) — you must scan all elements to confirm the minimum
O(log n) — you traverse a path from root to leaf
O(1) — the minimum is always at index 0 of the backing array
O(log n) — the heap must be partially sorted first
quiz.explanation: The min-heap property guarantees that the parent is always less than or equal to its children, so the global minimum is always at the root — index 0 in the array. Reading a specific array index is O(1).

quiz.question: After extracting the root from a min-heap, which sequence of steps correctly restores the heap?
options: Re-sort the entire array using comparison sort — O(n log n)
Move the last array element to index 0, then heapify-down by swapping with the smaller child until the heap property is restored — O(log n)
Find the new minimum by scanning all elements, then bubble it to the root — O(n)
Rebuild the entire heap from scratch using the O(n) heapify algorithm
quiz.explanation: Placing the last element at the root preserves the complete-tree structural property (no gap is created). Heapify-down then restores the ordering property by sifting the misplaced root down along the path where it causes the smallest violation, taking at most O(log n) swaps.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from an unsorted array of n elements using the optimal algorithm?
options: O(n²)
O(n log n) — same as sorting
O(n) — via sift-down from the last non-leaf to the root
O(log n)
quiz.explanation: Starting heapify-down at the last non-leaf (index n/2 - 1) and working backward to the root, the total work sums to O(n). Most nodes are near the bottom and sift down a small distance; the few nodes near the top sift farther but there are exponentially fewer of them. The series n/4×1 + n/8×2 + n/16×3 + … converges to O(n).

quiz.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a binary search tree from a binary heap?
options: A heap supports O(log n) search for arbitrary values; a BST only supports O(1) search
A BST enforces a full ordering invariant enabling in-order sorted traversal; a heap enforces only a parent-child ordering, enabling O(1) min/max access but not arbitrary sorted traversal
A heap must store values in sorted order; a BST stores values in insertion order
A BST is always stored as an array; a heap always uses pointer-based nodes
quiz.explanation: The BST property creates a globally consistent ordering (in-order traversal is sorted), while the heap property only guarantees parent vs. children — siblings can be in any relative order. This is why heaps support O(1) peek but cannot produce sorted output without O(n log n) repeated extraction.

quiz.question: Pre-order traversal (node → left → right) is most naturally suited for which task?
options: Producing sorted output from a BST
Computing directory sizes or expression values bottom-up
Serialising or cloning a tree structure — the root is recorded before its subtrees
Finding the shortest path to a leaf node
quiz.explanation: Pre-order visits the root before its children. If you record the visited values, you can reconstruct the exact same BST by re-inserting them in pre-order. For cloning, you create the parent node before recursing into children. Post-order (children before parent) is suited to deletion and bottom-up aggregation.

quiz.question: You have a stream of n numbers and need the k largest values efficiently. Which approach gives O(n log k) time?
options: Sort all n numbers in descending order and take the first k — O(n log n)
Use a max-heap of all n numbers and call pop() k times — O(n + k log n)
Maintain a min-heap of size k; for each new number, if it exceeds the heap minimum, pop the minimum and push the new number — O(n log k)
Use a BST and perform an in-order traversal taking the last k nodes — O(n)
quiz.explanation: A min-heap of size k tracks the k largest seen so far. Its root is the smallest of those k values. For each incoming element: if it is larger than the root, swap it in (O(log k)). Processing all n elements costs O(n log k), which is much faster than O(n log n) when k is small (e.g. top-10 from a million records).
